title: Kena Upanishad (one week): who impels the mind? (5 of 7)
word: the story of the gods and Brahman
hook: the gods win a victory and take the credit; then a stranger appears
tomorrow: Kena Upanishad (one week): who impels the mind? (6 of 7)

segments.voice: Yesterday: it is unknown to those who claim to know it. Your line, the one behind the ear. Did you leave a little room around something you were sure of? Day two hundred forty-three.

Picture a team that just won the championship. The locker room is loud. Everyone's giving interviews. I made that shot. My defense won it. Nobody mentions the coach who built the plan, or the groundskeeper, or the thousand things that had to go right. After two sections of paradox, the Kena changes gear completely. It tells a story. And it starts in a locker room, more or less: the gods have just won a great victory, and they're very pleased with themselves.
screen: `THE CHAMPIONSHIP LOCKER ROOM.` → `I MADE THAT SHOT.` → `THE GODS, PLEASED WITH THEMSELVES.`

segments.voice: Section three. Brahman won a victory for the gods. The text doesn't say against whom; tradition says the asuras, the gods' old rivals. But the gods felt great in that victory, and they said: this victory is ours, this greatness is ours. You can hear it. Ours. Brahman knew what they were thinking, and appeared before them. Not as a voice from heaven. As a yaksha: a wondrous, mysterious being, a presence they couldn't place. And they didn't know what it was. So they turned to Agni, the god of fire, the one who knows all beings. Agni, find out what this wondrous being is. Agni ran up to it. The being asked: who are you? I am Agni. I am the one who knows all beings. And what power is in you? I could burn up everything there is, whatever is on this earth. The being set down a single blade of grass. Burn this. Agni rushed at it with all his speed, and couldn't burn it. He came back to the gods: I couldn't find out what this being is. Stop there, because this is the heart of the story, and of the week's word. Fire, who can burn the world, can't burn a blade of grass. Why? Go back to the teaching. Brahman is the fire of fire, the one by which fire burns. Agni's power was never his own. It was on loan. When the one it came from simply held it back, there was nothing left. The story is the Kena's earlier teaching, acted out: the eye of the eye, now as a blade of grass.
screen: `THE VICTORY IS OURS.` · `A WONDROUS BEING APPEARS.` · `I COULD BURN THE WHOLE EARTH.` · `ONE BLADE OF GRASS.` · then, large: `FIRE CANNOT BURN IT.`

segments.voice: Two minutes. Think of something you're proud of: a skill, a win, a talent. Let yourself feel good about it. Now, gently, list what it rested on. Your body working. The people who taught you. The breath you didn't earn. The chance to be born at all. Let the pride stay, but let it widen into thanks. Breathe in: this is mine. Breathe out: this was given. The bell holds the time.
The story of the gods and Brahman. Today it began: the gods take the credit, a wondrous being appears, and fire can't burn a blade of grass.
screen: `THE STORY OF THE GODS AND BRAHMAN — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the one behind the ear. Today, when you're tempted to say, I did this, add silently: with help. Day two hundred forty-three.

howItsDone: The Kena's story of Agni and the blade of grass is often retold in Hindu teaching and children's storybooks as a lesson that every power comes from Brahman, and about the danger of pride.

fork.setup: you're Agni, god of fire. a stranger sets down one blade of grass and says: burn this. what happens?
options: you can't burn it, no matter how hard you try.
fork.reveal: Agni rushed at it with all his speed and couldn't burn it. his power had never been his own.

original.note: Sanskrit: yaksha, a wondrous or mysterious being; the form Brahman takes before the proud gods.

trapdoor: what you thought: it's a fable about a weak fire god.
what it means: Agni's power was lent; when its source held back, there was nothing left.
what a scholar hears: Kena 3 shifts from verse to prose; Agni calls himself jatavedas, knower of all beings, and his boast is the whole earth.
